title: Activities and hobbies
title_target: 你喜欢做什么 — Nǐ xǐhuan zuò shénme
goal: Build action sentences in subject–verb–object order, say what you like and dislike, and use adverbs of frequency — the part of Mandarin that's closest to English and so the quickest to master.
bekal: say what you like and dislike with 喜欢
use 常常, 有时候, 从来不
pair each verb with the right object (打球, 看书, 听音乐)
say something is in progress with 在

dialogs.title: 对话 1 — The weekend
dialogs.intro: Wang Li and Andi chat about their daily activities. Notice that the word order is exactly the same as in English — this is the friendliest part of Mandarin for us.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: What do you usually do on weekends?
lines.literal: you — week-end — often — do — what.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [我|Wǒ][喜欢|xǐhuan][看|kàn][电影|diànyǐng]，[也|yě][喜欢|xǐhuan][做饭|zuò fàn]。
lines.id: I like watching movies, and I like cooking too.
lines.literal: I — like — look — movie, also — like — make — rice.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Can you cook Chinese food?
lines.literal: you — can — make — China — dish — (question).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: A little. I often make fried rice.
lines.literal: can — a-little. I — often — make — fry-rice.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Do you like sports?
lines.literal: you — like — move-body — (question).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [喜欢|Xǐhuan]。[我|Wǒ][每|měi][个|ge][星期|xīngqī][打|dǎ][两|liǎng][次|cì][羽毛球|yǔmáoqiú]。
lines.id: I do. I play badminton twice a week.
lines.literal: like. I — every — (classifier) — week — hit — two — times — feather-ball.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Great! I never exercise.
lines.literal: truly — good. I — ever-since — not — exercise.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: So what do you usually do?
lines.literal: that — you — ordinary-time — do — what.

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.text: [看|Kàn][书|shū]，[听|tīng][音乐|yīnyuè]，[有时候|yǒu shíhou][跟|gēn][朋友|péngyou][聊天儿|liáotiānr]。
lines.id: Read, listen to music, sometimes chat with friends.
lines.literal: look — book, listen — music, have — time — with — friend — chat.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [下|Xià][个|ge][星期天|xīngqītiān][我们|wǒmen][一起|yìqǐ][打|dǎ][球|qiú][吧|ba]！
lines.id: Let's play ball together next Sunday!
lines.literal: below — (classifier) — week-sky — we — together — hit — ball — (suggestion).

lines.speaker: 王丽:
lines.id: Sure! But I'm not good at it.
lines.literal: good — (softener). but — I — hit — (marker) — not — good.

notes: **Mandarin action sentences follow exactly the same order as English: subject – verb – object.** [我看书|Wǒ kàn shū] I read books. Nothing to flip, nothing to memorize. The only part that differs from English is **adverbials**, which always stand before the verb.

**[喜欢|xǐhuan] can be followed by a noun or a verb.** [我喜欢咖啡|Wǒ xǐhuan kāfēi] I like coffee; [我喜欢看电影|Wǒ xǐhuan kàn diànyǐng] I like watching movies. ⚠️ There's no "to" or "-ing" in between — don't add anything.
**[会|huì] = can, because you've learned how.** [我会做饭|Wǒ huì zuò fàn] I can cook; [我会说中文|Wǒ huì shuō Zhōngwén] I can speak Mandarin. This is different from [能|néng], covered in Unit 9.

**⚠️ Adverbs of frequency stand BEFORE the verb**: [常常|chángcháng] often, [有时候|yǒu shíhou] sometimes, [从来不|cónglái bù] never, [每天|měi tiān] every day. An order like "I exercise often" doesn't exist in Mandarin.
**How many times: number + [次|cì], placed AFTER the verb.** [我打两次球|Wǒ dǎ liǎng cì qiú] or [我一个星期打两次羽毛球|Wǒ yí ge xīngqī dǎ liǎng cì yǔmáoqiú]. This is one of the few things that come after the verb.

**[从来不|cónglái bù] = never (habit), [从来没|cónglái méi] = have never (experience).** [我从来不喝酒|Wǒ cónglái bù hē jiǔ] I never drink alcohol (that's my habit); [我从来没去过中国|Wǒ cónglái méi qù guo Zhōngguó] I've never been to China.
**[打得不好|dǎ de bù hǎo] = plays badly.** This verb + [得|de] + judgment pattern is HSK 3 material, but you'll hear it all the time. Recognize the form now; master it later.

grammars.title: Verbs and their objects — pairs that belong together
body: Mandarin is very picky about which verb goes with which object. Memorizing a verb on its own is almost useless; memorize the **pair**.
after: ⚠️ **[打|dǎ] for balls you hit with a hand or racket, [踢|tī] for balls you kick.** Badminton, basketball, table tennis: 打. Soccer: 踢. Mixing them up sounds funny right away.
⚠️ If there's no particular object, many Mandarin verbs carry a built-in one: [吃饭|chī fàn] literally "eat rice" but simply means "eat"; [说话|shuō huà] "talk"; [睡觉|shuì jiào] "sleep".

grammars.title: How often

head: Mandarin
Meaning
Example
rows: [我常常看电影|Wǒ chángcháng kàn diànyǐng]。
[我有时候做饭|Wǒ yǒu shíhou zuò fàn]。
[我很少喝酒|Wǒ hěn shǎo hē jiǔ]。
[我从来不抽烟|Wǒ cónglái bù chōu yān]。
[我每天学中文|Wǒ měi tiān xué Zhōngwén]。
[一个星期两次|yí ge xīngqī liǎng cì]

after: Every word in the left column stands **before the verb**, except [次|cì], which stands **after** it. When a sentence has both, the order is: time → how often → verb → how many times → object. [我一个星期打两次球|Wǒ yí ge xīngqī dǎ liǎng cì qiú].

dialogs.title: 对话 2 — What are you doing?
dialogs.intro: Andi calls Li Ming during work hours. Notice how Mandarin says that something is in progress — far simpler than you'd expect.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: Hello, Li Ming! What are you up to?
lines.literal: hello, Li Ming. you — (in progress) — do — what.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: I'm in a meeting. What's up?
lines.literal: I — (in progress) — open — meeting. have — what — matter — (question).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [没|Méi][什么|shénme][急事|jíshì]。[你|Nǐ][几|jǐ][点|diǎn][下班|xià bān]？
lines.id: Nothing urgent. What time do you get off work?
lines.literal: not-have — what — urgent-matter. you — how-many — o'clock — go-down — shift.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Six. Why?
lines.literal: six — o'clock. how — (change).

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [晚上|Wǎnshang][有|yǒu][一|yí][个|ge][中国|Zhōngguó][电影|diànyǐng]。[你|Nǐ][想|xiǎng][看|kàn][吗|ma]？
lines.id: There's a Chinese movie tonight. Want to see it?
lines.literal: evening — have — one — (classifier) — China — movie. you — want — look — (question).

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.text: [什么|Shénme][电影|diànyǐng]？[我|Wǒ][不太|bú tài][喜欢|xǐhuan][爱情片|àiqíngpiàn]。
lines.id: What movie? I'm not really into romance films.
lines.literal: what — movie. I — not-too — like — love-feeling-film.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.id: No, it's a kung fu movie. I hear it's good.
lines.literal: not — be, be — kungfu-film. hear-say — (link) — good-to-look-at.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: Then I'm in! What time does it start?
lines.literal: that — I — go. how-many — o'clock — start.

lines.speaker: 安迪:
lines.text: [七|Qī][点|diǎn][半|bàn]。[我们|Wǒmen][七|qī][点|diǎn][在|zài][电影院|diànyǐngyuàn][门口|ménkǒu][见|jiàn]。
lines.id: Seven thirty. Let's meet at seven outside the cinema.
lines.literal: seven — o'clock — half. we — seven — o'clock — at — movie-hall — door — meet.

lines.speaker: 李明:
lines.id: No problem. See you later!
lines.literal: not-have — problem. a-while — see.

notes: **[喂|wéi] is the "hello" for phone calls**, and only for phone calls. The second tone (*wéi*) sounds friendly; the fourth tone (*wèi*) sounds like calling someone from far away.

**[在|zài] + verb = in progress (-ing).** [我在开会|Wǒ zài kāi huì] I'm in a meeting. Yes — the same word as "be at" from Unit 6. How to tell them apart: if a **place** follows, it means "at"; if a **verb** follows, it means "-ing". The stronger form [正在|zhèngzài] is also common.
**[不太|bú tài] + adjective = "not very …".** [不太好|bú tài hǎo] not very good, [不太喜欢|bú tài xǐhuan] not really like. This is how Mandarin says no gently — much more polite than 不喜欢, which sounds blunt.
**[听说|tīngshuō] = "I hear, they say".** It always stands at the front of the sentence: [听说很好看|Tīngshuō hěn hǎokàn] I hear it's good.

**[好看|hǎokàn] literally "good to look at".** The pattern [好|hǎo] + a sense verb makes an adjective: [好听|hǎotīng] nice to hear, [好吃|hǎochī] tasty (food), [好喝|hǎohē] tasty (drinks), [好玩儿|hǎowánr] fun. ⚠️ Never use 好吃 for drinks — for drinks it's always 好喝.
**[怎么了|Zěnme le]？ = "what's wrong? what's up?"** — asks about a situation or problem. Different from [怎么|zěnme] alone, which means "how".
**[一会儿见|Yíhuìr jiàn]！** = see you later (within a few hours).

grammars.title: Saying something is in progress

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: He's eating. — the most casual form
[他在看书呢|Tā zài kàn shū ne]。
[他没在开会|Tā méi zài kāi huì]。

after: ⚠️ Mandarin **doesn't require** this marker. [他吃饭|Tā chī fàn] can already mean "he's eating" when the context is clear. Use 在 when you want to **stress** that the action is ongoing — for example, to explain why you can't talk right now.

Pīnyīn
Activity

blocks.title: Saying what you like and dislike
items: [我很喜欢…|Wǒ hěn xǐhuan…] — I really like …
[我喜欢…|Wǒ xǐhuan…] — I like …
[还可以|Hái kěyǐ]。 — It's okay. (neutral, often used to dodge the question)
[我不太喜欢…|Wǒ bú tài xǐhuan…] — I'm not really into … (gentle no)
[我不喜欢…|Wǒ bù xǐhuan…] — I don't like … (blunt)
[我最喜欢…|Wǒ zuì xǐhuan…] — What I like most is …
⚠️ In Chinese conversation, a flat refusal comes across as rather harsh. [不太|bú tài] is almost always the better choice.

blocks.text: Phoning in a foreign language is harder than talking face to face: no faces, no hands, nothing written down. The sentences below are a frame you can hold on to.

head: Sentence
Meaning
rows: [请问，王丽在吗|Qǐngwèn, Wáng Lì zài ma]？
Excuse me, is Wang Li there?
This is Andi. — ⚠️ not 我叫; on the phone you use 我是
[我一会儿再打|Wǒ yíhuìr zài dǎ]。

blocks.title: 打电话 — the verb is 打
items: [给我打电话|gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà] — call me. Note the order: **给 + person + 打电话**, not 打电话给我.
[我给妈妈打电话|Wǒ gěi māma dǎ diànhuà]。 — I call my mom.
[接电话|jiē diànhuà] answer the phone · [挂电话|guà diànhuà] hang up.
[发信息|fā xìnxī] send a message · [加微信|jiā Wēixìn] add someone on WeChat.
[你的微信号是多少|Nǐ de Wēixìn hào shì duōshao]？ — What's your WeChat ID? A question you'll hear at every introduction in China.

exercises.prompt: Correct these sentences, then write the correct form in pīnyīn.
items: [我看电影常常|Wǒ kàn diànyǐng chángcháng]。
[我喜欢是看书|Wǒ xǐhuan shì kàn shū]。
[他打足球|Tā dǎ zúqiú]。
[这个咖啡很好吃|Zhège kāfēi hěn hǎochī]。

answers: 看 — 听 — 打 — 踢 — 做 — 喝
每天 — 从来不 — 常常 — 很少 — 有时候
我 喜欢 看 中国 电影 — 我 每天 晚上 听 音乐 — 他 从来 不 运动 — 我 一个星期 打 两 次 球 — 你 会 做 中国菜 吗 — 我 在 开会 呢
On weekends I often read at home. — What do you like to do? — I'm not really into dancing. — He's on the phone. — I hear this movie is good.
Wǒ xǐhuan tīng yīnyuè. — Wǒ měi tiān xué Zhōngwén. — Tā zài chī fàn. — Nǐ huì zuò fàn ma? — Wǒ yí ge xīngqī yóu liǎng cì yǒng.
Wǒ chángcháng kàn diànyǐng. — Wǒ xǐhuan kàn shū. — Tā tī zúqiú. — Zhège kāfēi hěn hǎohē. — Wǒ yí ge xīngqī dǎ liǎng cì qiú.
wave: Review Unit 6: walk around your home and name what you usually do in each room — with the place and how often. [我常常在客厅看电视|Wǒ chángcháng zài kètīng kàn diànshì]。 Places and habits, practiced together.
